S027.name: Sleep_Disturbance
S027.description: A state where there is a significant change in the quantity or quality of sleep.

subtypes.Initial Insomnia: Difficulty falling asleep and taking a long time to do so.
subtypes.Middle Insomnia: Waking up frequently during sleep or having difficulty falling back asleep.
subtypes.Early Morning Awakening: Waking up too early and being unable to fall back asleep.
subtypes.Hypersomnia: Sleeping for long periods at night or excessive sleep during the day.
subtypes.Nightmare Disorder: Sleep disturbance caused by repeated and distressing dreams.
subtypes.Non-Restorative Sleep: Feeling unrefreshed despite having slept enough.

S069.name: Intrusive_Symptoms
S069.description: Recurrent, involuntary, and intrusive distressing memories of the traumatic event.

subtypes.Intrusive Memories: Recurrent, involuntary, and intrusive distressing memories of the traumatic event.
subtypes.Distressing Dreams: Recurrent distressing dreams in which the content and/or affect of the dream are related to the traumatic event.
subtypes.Dissociative Reactions (Flashbacks): Dissociative reactions (e.g., flashbacks) in which the individual feels or acts as if the traumatic event were recurring.
subtypes.Psychological Distress at Cues: Intense or prolonged psychological distress at exposure to internal or external cues that symbolize or resemble an aspect of the traumatic event.
subtypes.Physiological Reactions to Cues: Marked physiological reactions to internal or external cues that symbolize or resemble an aspect of the traumatic event.

S070.name: Trauma_Avoidance
S070.description: Persistent avoidance of stimuli associated with the traumatic event.

subtypes.Internal Avoidance: Efforts to avoid distressing memories, thoughts, or feelings about or closely associated with the traumatic event.
subtypes.External Avoidance: Efforts to avoid external reminders (people, places, conversations, activities, objects, situations) that arouse distressing memories, thoughts, or feelings.

S071.name: Trauma_Related_Amnesia
S071.description: Inability to remember an important aspect of the traumatic event (typically due to dissociative amnesia and not to other factors like head injury or alcohol).

subtypes.Fragmented Memory: Inability to recall only specific parts of the traumatic event while remembering others.
subtypes.Generalized Amnesia: Inability to recall the majority or the entirety of the traumatic event.

S072.name: Negative_Beliefs
S072.description: Persistent and exaggerated negative beliefs or expectations about oneself, others, or the world.

subtypes.Negative Self-Beliefs: Distorted beliefs such as 'I am fundamentally bad,' 'I am damaged,' or 'I am worthless'.
subtypes.Negative Beliefs about Others: Distorted beliefs such as 'No one can be trusted' or 'Others are dangerous'.
subtypes.Negative Worldview: Extreme beliefs such as 'The world is completely dangerous' or 'Life is meaningless'.

S075.name: Social_Detachment
S075.description: Feelings of detachment or estrangement from others.

subtypes.Emotional Detachment: Feeling cut off from others even when physically present, unable to feel connection.
subtypes.Social Isolation: Increasingly isolating oneself and not participating in social activities or gatherings.
subtypes.Difficulty with Intimacy: Distancing oneself from close people as it is difficult to become emotionally close.
subtypes.Loss of Belonging: Feeling like an outsider who belongs nowhere.

S076.name: Inability_Positive_Emotions
S076.description: Persistent inability to experience positive emotions (e.g., inability to experience happiness, satisfaction, or loving feelings).

subtypes.Anhedonia for Happiness: Unable to feel happiness or joy even when good things happen.
subtypes.Lack of Satisfaction: Unable to experience satisfaction or pride even after achieving something good.
subtypes.Inability to Feel Love: Feeling numb to love or affection towards family or lovers.
subtypes.Emotional Numbness: A state where the mind feels empty and nothing is felt, as if all positive emotions are blocked.

S077.name: Irritability_Aggression
S077.description: Irritable behavior and angry outbursts (with little or no provocation) typically expressed as verbal or physical aggression.

subtypes.Impulsive Anger: Sudden explosions of anger for trivial reasons or no clear reason.
subtypes.Verbal Aggression: Attacking others with shouting, cursing, or blame without holding back.
subtypes.Physical Aggression: Physically attacking people or throwing/breaking objects.
subtypes.Chronic Irritability: A state where nerves are always sharp and sensitive, ready to explode at the slightest touch.

S079.name: Hypervigilance
S079.description: Persistent state of being alert and tense about the surrounding environment.

subtypes.Scanning for Danger: Always scanning the surroundings and being alert to find potential threats or risks.
subtypes.Safety Checking: Repetitively confirming safety, such as checking exit locations or observing people around.
subtypes.Sustained Alertness: Unable to relax tension even in safe environments and maintaining a constant state of alertness.

S080.name: Exaggerated_Startle_Response
S080.description: Exaggerated startle response to minor stimuli.

subtypes.Auditory Startle: Startling excessively and flinching physically at sudden noises.
subtypes.Tactile Startle: Being extremely startled by unexpected physical contact.
subtypes.Visual Startle: Being greatly startled and wary of sudden appearances of people or rapid movements.
subtypes.Slow Recovery: Heart pounding and trembling for a long time after being startled, not calming down easily.

symptom.disease_info: Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) is a trauma- and stressor-related disorder that develops after exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence, either directly, as a witness, or through learning of it occurring to close others. It is characterized by persistent intrusive recollections of the event, avoidance of trauma-related cues, negative alterations in cognition and mood, and marked changes in arousal and reactivity lasting more than one month and causing significant impairment. The clinical course can be acute or chronic, with onset often within three months of the trauma but sometimes delayed, and symptoms may fluctuate in intensity over time. PTSD is distinguished from other anxiety and mood disorders by the requirement of a qualifying traumatic event and the specific pattern of re-experiencing, avoidance, and hyperarousal linked to that event.

patient.personality: Dianna is a practical, organized, and quietly generous person who enjoys learning, nature, and nurturing community connections through hobbies and volunteering.
patient.stressor: Dianna’s PTSD developed after she suffered a sudden cardiac arrest while hiking with her husband; she collapsed on the trail, stopped breathing, and required prolonged CPR from a bystander and a chaotic emergency helicopter evacuation before being resuscitated in the hospital. Surviving what she experienced as coming close to death profoundly shook her previously steady, solution-focused outlook, and returning home did not bring the relief she expected, as everyday bodily sensations and environmental noises began to feel ominously tied to that day on the trail. Over the following 19 months, she forced herself to maintain her meticulous performance at the insurance office and her caregiving roles, yet the lingering fear associated with medical settings, emergency sirens, and even vigorous activity led her to abandon hiking groups, withdraw from some volunteer work, and avoid certain social gatherings where health scares were discussed. When her exaggerated reactions to small sounds—like dropped objects at work or ambulance sirens passing by—started to draw worried comments from coworkers and made it increasingly hard for her to participate in bridge games or book club meetings without embarrassment, she accepted a referral from her primary care physician for psychiatric evaluation.
patient.chief_complaint: “Lately I jump out of my skin at the smallest noise, like something terrible is about to happen again.”

S027.name: Sleep_Disturbance
S027.description: A state where there is a significant change in the quantity or quality of sleep.
S027.manifestation: Most nights I lie there for hours listening to my heartbeat and every little creak in the house, doze off for a bit, then bolt awake from the same kind of nightmare where I’m back on that trail not breathing, and by morning I feel like I haven’t slept at all even if I was technically in bed all night.

S069.name: Intrusive_Symptoms
S069.description: Recurrent, involuntary, and intrusive distressing memories of the traumatic event.
S069.manifestation: Out of nowhere—at my desk, in the grocery store, even in church—I’ll suddenly see myself on the ground again, people shouting, the helicopter blades roaring, and for a few seconds it feels like I’m right back there about to die, with my chest tightening and my hands shaking so badly I have to stop what I’m doing.

S070.name: Trauma_Avoidance
S070.description: Persistent avoidance of stimuli associated with the traumatic event.
S070.manifestation: I go out of my way to steer clear of anything that reminds me of that day, so I’ve quit the hiking club, I won’t walk the aisles with the defibrillators at work, I mute TV shows with medical scenes, and if people start talking about heart problems or ambulances I make an excuse to leave the room because I can’t stand how it makes me feel.

S071.name: Trauma_Related_Amnesia
S071.description: Inability to remember an important aspect of the traumatic event (typically due to dissociative amnesia and not to other factors like head injury or alcohol).
S071.manifestation: I can remember collapsing and then waking up in the hospital, but there are big empty patches around the CPR and the helicopter ride that everyone else describes in detail, and when I try to picture it my mind just sort of blanks out like it’s a movie with missing scenes.

S072.name: Negative_Beliefs
S072.description: Persistent and exaggerated negative beliefs or expectations about oneself, others, or the world.
S072.manifestation: Ever since this happened I can’t shake the thought that my body is a ticking time bomb and that nothing is really safe anymore, so I walk around expecting something awful to happen again and feeling like I was foolish to ever believe I could just be a healthy, normal person.

S075.name: Social_Detachment
S075.description: Feelings of detachment or estrangement from others.
S075.manifestation: Even when I’m sitting at book club or in the office surrounded by people I’ve known for years, I feel like I’m watching from behind a glass wall, nodding and smiling on the outside but completely cut off and alone on the inside because no one really understands how far away I feel from my old life.

S076.name: Inability_Positive_Emotions
S076.description: Persistent inability to experience positive emotions (e.g., inability to experience happiness, satisfaction, or loving feelings).
S076.manifestation: When my granddaughter runs up to hug me or my coworkers throw me a little birthday celebration, I go through the motions and say the right things, but inside it’s like I’m numb and hollow, unable to actually feel happy or grateful the way I know I’m supposed to.

S077.name: Irritability_Aggression
S077.description: Irritable behavior and angry outbursts (with little or no provocation) typically expressed as verbal or physical aggression.
S077.manifestation: I’ve turned into this snappy, short-tempered person where the tiniest things—like my husband misplacing the remote or a coworker asking a routine question—set me off yelling or speaking so sharply that I see the hurt on their faces and then feel awful, but I can’t seem to stop myself in the moment.

S079.name: Hypervigilance
S079.description: Persistent state of being alert and tense about the surrounding environment.
S079.manifestation: I’m constantly on edge, always checking where the exits are, listening for sirens, monitoring how my chest feels, and even at home I find myself pacing around or sitting rigidly upright because relaxing makes me feel like I’m letting my guard down and something bad will sneak up on me.

S080.name: Exaggerated_Startle_Response
S080.description: Exaggerated startle response to minor stimuli.
S080.manifestation: If a file drawer slams at work or an ambulance goes by the window, I literally jump out of my chair with my heart pounding, my whole body jolting like I’ve been shocked, and it takes several minutes of deep breathing before I can stop shaking and pretend everything’s normal again.
